subject: biochemistry
title: Extracellular matrix biochemistry: collagen biosynthesis, lysyl oxidase and connective tissue disorders

steps.tx: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, characterized by a **triple-helix** quaternary structure composed of three polypeptide alpha chains. The primary sequence contains a strict Glycine-X-Y repeating motif, where glycine occurs every third residue. Because glycine is the smallest amino acid with only a single hydrogen atom side chain, it fits neatly into the restricted central axis of the tightly coiled triple helix.
steps.say: Collagen is the body's most abundant protein, featuring a triple helix of three alpha chains. It has a strict Glycine-X-Y repeating sequence where glycine occupies every third position. Because glycine is the smallest amino acid, it fits inside the crowded central axis of the triple helix.

rows: Blood vessels, uterus, fetal skin, granulation

steps.tx: The close view shows three wound strands with tiny beads packed inside. Every third position holds a small **glycine** at the center, giving the strict **Gly X Y repeat** of the **triple helix**. Proline and hydroxyproline sit outside and steady the coil. This explains why any bulky swap for glycine wrecks collagen structure.
steps.say: The model shows three chains coiled together with glycine buried in the middle. Labels mark the repeating pattern plus proline and hydroxyproline on the outside. Glycine fits because it is smallest. A larger residue in its place would distort the helix and weaken connective tissue.

steps.tx: Intracellular collagen processing begins in the rough endoplasmic reticulum with signal peptide cleavage. Prolyl and lysyl **hydroxylases** hydroxylate specific proline and lysine residues, requiring vitamin C (ascorbate), molecular oxygen, ferrous iron, and alpha-ketoglutarate as cofactors. Selected hydroxylysine residues undergo glycosylation with glucose and galactose. Triple-helix assembly initiates at the carboxy-terminus, stabilized by interchain disulfide bonds to form soluble procollagen.
steps.say: Intracellular collagen assembly starts in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases modify residues using vitamin C, iron, and oxygen. Hydroxylysines undergo glycosylation. Disulfide bonds at the carboxy-terminus initiate triple-helix winding to create procollagen.

steps.tx: Extracellularly, procollagen peptidases cleave non-helical **terminal** propeptides, converting soluble procollagen into insoluble tropocollagen. Tropocollagen molecules self-assemble into staggered parallel fibrils. The copper-dependent extracellular enzyme lysyl oxidase oxidatively deaminates lysine and hydroxylysine residues into reactive allysine aldehydes. Spontaneous aldol condensations between adjacent aldehydes create covalent crosslinks, conferring immense tensile strength to the mature collagen fibril.
steps.say: Extracellular procollagen peptidases cleave terminal propeptides, yielding insoluble tropocollagen that self-assembles into fibrils. The copper-dependent enzyme lysyl oxidase deaminates lysine into allysine aldehydes. These form covalent crosslinks, conferring tensile strength to mature collagen.

left.title: Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency)
points: Failure of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation
Unstable triple-helix degrades at body temperature
Gingival bleeding, hemarthrosis, impaired wound healing

right.title: Menkes disease (Copper deficiency)
points: ATP7A mutation impairs intestinal copper transport
Arterial aneurysms, kinky hair, developmental delay

steps.tx: Genetic disorders of the extracellular matrix compromise tissue **integrity**. Osteogenesis imperfecta results from COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations that replace invariant glycine with bulky amino acids, causing dominant-negative disruption of type I collagen triple helices, manifesting as bone fractures and blue sclerae. Marfan syndrome is caused by FBN1 mutations in fibrillin-1, an extracellular glycoprotein microfibril that forms a scaffold for elastin, causing aortic root aneurysm.
steps.say: Matrix gene mutations produce severe clinical syndromes. Osteogenesis imperfecta results from type I collagen glycine substitutions, causing multiple bone fractures and blue sclerae. Marfan syndrome stems from fibrillin-1 mutations, disrupting elastin microfibrils and predisposing to aortic dissection.

rows: Decreased synthesis of normal Type I
Multiple fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss
Lethal in perinatal period, crumpling fractures

steps.tx: The eye shows a diffuse blue grey tint across the sclera. Thin sclera lets dark inner layers show through in **osteogenesis imperfecta**, where faulty **type I collagen** from glycine swaps weakens bone and eye wall. Seeing **blue sclerae** with fractures should trigger recall of dominant collagen defects rather than simple bruising.
steps.say: The photo shows a pale blue wash over the white of the eye. In osteogenesis imperfecta, abnormal type one collagen makes sclera thin so pigment beneath shows through. The same weak collagen breaks easily. Blue sclera plus repeated fractures points to this diagnosis.
